role: Dental assistant at a chain clinic
headline: Out of nursing school with a dental track, you landed at a neighborhood branch of a Xuzhou dental chain: suction, mixing, passing instruments and sterilizing at Chair 3, booked solid on weekends, off only on Mondays
unit: A neighborhood branch of a dental chain in Xuzhou, six chairs
level: You can recite the name of every instrument but your hands don't know the materials yet; no nursing license, and half the dentist's gestures still mean nothing to you
intro: The clinic on Pengcheng Road has six chairs. You are assigned to Chair 3, beside a dentist with more than ten years of root canals behind him. You studied dental nursing at a vocational school and haven't passed the license exam, so for now you suction, mix materials, pass instruments and run the sterilizer. The dentist's hand reaches out without a word. Your job is to have the thing there before it does.
salary_note: Estimate: base pay for private dental assistants in Xuzhou is low, and income leans on weekend overtime and package commissions, about 20 percent below the same job in Nanjing.

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the job database is mostly campus hiring and internships)

day: The light in the sterilization room comes on first. You peel off the printout from last night's load, stick it in the log, check that the indicator card has fully turned, and only then shelve the packs.
First up is a thirty-nine-yuan group-buy cleaning. You hang the suction tube and set the chair. The sales consultant is already waiting in the doorway for the patient to finish rinsing.
Root canal at Chair 3. The dentist's left hand opens behind him and you lay a size 15 file in it. It's the first time today he hasn't looked back.
Changing gloves, you find the web of your thumb has split again. Braised pork over rice downstairs, fifteen yuan. As you eat, the thin whine of the high-speed handpiece is still in your ears.
A seven-year-old gets his mouth half open and starts crying. You hold up the suction tube and let him touch it, and tell him it's a little elephant trunk that drinks water. His father films this.
Alginate impression: thirty seconds to get it into the tray. Summer water sets it too fast, so you swap in some from the fridge.

The chairs wiped down one by one; instruments soaked in enzyme, run through the ultrasonic, dried, pouched. The dentist has long gone. The sterilizer starts building pressure, and you have to wait out the cycle.

ladder.title: Trainee Dental Assistant
ladder.focus: Learn instruments, sterilization and chairside suction; you can't work a chair alone until your trainer signs off

ladder.title: Dental Assistant
ladder.focus: Run four-handed work with one dentist, mix materials, take impressions, manage the chair and follow-up calls

ladder.title: Senior Dental Assistant
ladder.focus: Assist on implants and orthodontics, train new hires, keep the clinic's infection-control records

ladder.title: Clinic Nursing Supervisor
ladder.focus: Scheduling, inventory and inspections, wedged between dentists, consultants and the branch manager

ladder.title: Regional Nursing Inspector
ladder.focus: Tour several branches, set procedures, audit infection control and train staff, answerable for the group's quality metrics

ai_tasks.name: Working chairside with the dentist
ai_tasks.how: The angle of the suction, the timing of each instrument, what to do when a patient panics: all of it happens at the chair. AI can't reach into a patient's mouth.

ai_tasks.name: Calming frightened patients
ai_tasks.how: Whether a seven-year-old opens his mouth depends on the person in front of him.

ai_tasks.name: Scheduling and recall reminders
ai_tasks.how: Filling chairs, sending reminders and plugging gaps: the system is already faster than the front desk.

ai_tasks.name: Cleaning up intraoral scans
ai_tasks.how: AI can stitch scans, patch holes and find margins. Someone still has to check the margins and the bite against the actual mouth.

ai_tasks.name: First-pass marks on X-rays
ai_tasks.how: Software can circle suspect areas on a CBCT. Whether they are right and need treatment is the dentist's call; the assistant has to explain the circles to the patient.

ai_tasks.name: Sterilization and supply records
ai_tasks.how: Barcodes can track every pack's batch and destination. Whether it's sealed properly and whether anyone read the indicator is still a person's job.

events.e_cement: The first time you mix glass ionomer alone, the powder runs a little heavy and it sets on the spatula before you can hand it over. The dentist says “Again” in the voice he uses for “Next.” That night you practice the wrist motion on the glass slab until the sterilizer finishes.
events.e_four_hands: A root canal runs forty minutes. From start to finish the dentist says nothing and never waits for an instrument. Afterward he asks how old you are. Twenty-one, you say. He says, all right.
events.e_bio_test: The weekly biological indicator comes back changed color. Without waiting for the manager you pull every pack sterilized since that load and rerun them, and spend the morning on eleven phone calls rescheduling. The afternoon retest is negative; the vial had simply been stored too long. The manager says pulling them was right.
events.e_inspection: The health commission shows up unannounced for an infection-control check, walks straight into the sterilization room and pages back three months in the log. Halfway through, the inspector asks why the handwriting is the same every single day. Because I wrote it every single day, you say.
events.e_gloves: A red rash spreads over your hands and itches whenever the gloves come off. It's a latex allergy. Nitrile costs several yuan more a box, and the manager wants you to cover the difference. You argue with him for two weeks.
events.e_tinnitus: Lying down at night, you hear a thin wire of sound, just under the pitch of the high-speed handpiece. Your audiogram sags at the high end. You start wearing the kind of earplugs that still let speech through, and the dentist complains you've gone half a beat slow.
events.e_neck: Assisting means leaning out to the left, and you've been leaning for over ten years. The film shows the space between your fifth and sixth cervical vertebrae has narrowed. You tape a rehab routine to the sterilization room wall and do two sets at lunch while colleagues edge past behind you.
events.e_summer: Summer vacation arrives and students with braces fill July. Follow-up after follow-up: new archwires, ligatures, photos, twenty-odd mouths a day. By the end of August you could say with your eyes closed what size elastics each kid wore last time.
events.e_groupon: The group-buy platform raises its cut by two points, and the clinic trims the thirty-nine-yuan cleaning from forty minutes to twenty-five. Whatever you can't finish, the next patient's stare reminds you of.
events.e_denture_old: An old man from Tongshan comes once a year to have his full dentures adjusted. Each time he brings a bag of his own sweet potatoes and asks for Chair 3. This year he brings no sweet potatoes. He brings his daughter-in-law, who asks how many more years the teeth will last.
events.e_vbp: Volume-based procurement reaches dental implants, and one tooth drops from over ten thousand yuan to a little over six thousand. Within two months bookings run three months out, nearly all of them old people who have been putting it off for years. The dentists' commissions shrink, the cases multiply, and you assist until your fingers swell.
events.e_scanner: The clinic gets its first intraoral scanner. The impression trays slowly retire to the cupboard, and alginate orders fall by half. That thirty-second tray of yours now comes in useful only in mouths the scanner can't get into.
events.e_ai_marks: The imaging software updates, and AI starts circling suspect spots on the CBCT by itself. The consultant turns the screen toward the patient and red rings light up one after another. The patient turns to you: that many? You say the dentist will need to look.
events.e_sold: The chain is bought by a group from the south. New sign; the sterilization log becomes a barcode scan; the records migration loses two years of follow-up calls. Old patients at Chair 3 ask first if the owner has changed, and then whether their teeth still count.
events.e_prepaid: Another dental company in town shuts its doors, and dozens of its patients come in holding prepaid cards, asking if you'll honor them. You won't. You stand at the desk explaining this is a different company, one person at a time, until a woman lays her card on the counter and says, then whose tooth is this?
events.e_doctor_leaves: The dentist you've assisted for seven years quits to open his own practice, without asking you along. His replacement is left-handed. Your stance, your tray, all of it has to be reversed, and in the first month you pass him the wrong thing three times.
events.e_weekend: Weekends are the clinic's busiest days and the worst days for ferrying kids to tutoring. You and your spouse tape a schedule to the fridge; in a good month, the family gets one whole weekend together. On Monday afternoons you wait at the school gate among the grandparents.
events.e_own_teeth: House rule: staff get cleanings free. The first time you lie back in Chair 3 and look up at that lamp, you learn what the suction tube feels like against the back of the tongue. The next day you move it half a centimeter out.

c_upsell.title: The consultant's commission
c_upsell.situation: The sales consultant makes you an offer: patients trust you most when they're in the chair, so while you suction, mention that an all-ceramic crown beats porcelain-fused-to-metal, and you'll get ten percent of any sale. Your rent went up this month. And it isn't exactly a lie.

options.label: Mention it
options.result: You mention it. When the commissions land, you are less pleased than you'd expected, but the rent is paid. A woman later asks you whether her old crown is really no good.

options.label: Just do the suction
options.result: You say she should ask the dentist. From then on the consultant is polite and cool around the schedule. A few patients start asking for Chair 3 by name.

c_nurse.title: The nursing license
c_nurse.situation: Without a nursing license there are things you just don't get to do: preparing an anesthetic, assisting with an IV. To sit the exam you have to make up clinical rotation hours, which means three months' leave and no commission.

options.label: Take leave and do the hours
options.result: You spend three months in the surgical ward of a city hospital, your first time working where there are no dental chairs. Once you pass, your name moves to a different place on the schedule.

options.label: Skip it and keep earning
options.result: You keep assisting. Your hands are as good as anyone's, except that partway through some procedures, someone with a license has to be called in.

c_senior.title: Applying for Senior Dental Assistant
c_senior.situation: The region is naming a Senior Dental Assistant at your branch, to assist implant surgery, train new staff and keep the infection-control log. It means more weekends and two weeks of training in Nanjing, and the form has a box: willing to cover other branches?

options.label: Apply, and tick the box
options.result: You start shuttling between two clinics, reading implant instrument lists standing up on Xuzhou's Line 1. Your tray grows from a dozen instruments to more than forty.

options.label: Stay at Chair 3
options.result: The slot goes to someone from another branch. You keep Chair 3, the old patients keep asking for you, and you eat a few more dinners on weekends than the others do.

c_scan.title: Learning scanners and digital work
c_scan.situation: The group wants one digital specialist at each branch: intraoral scanning, AI cleanup, sending data to the lab. The training is after hours, with no raise, only an in-house certificate. Everyone else at the clinic says this should be the dentists' work anyway.

options.label: Learn it after work
options.result: You learn to read margins on a screen, and to distrust the smooth stretch AI has patched in. The lab technicians start calling you directly.

options.label: Your hands are enough
options.result: You stay the tray person. When a scan comes through bad, they remember you and ask for a real impression.

c_nanjing.title: The visiting surgeon's offer
c_nanjing.situation: The implant surgeon who comes up from Nanjing each month says his clinic there needs someone who can assist in surgery. The pay is thirty percent more. Your spouse and child are both in Xuzhou.

options.label: Go to Nanjing
options.result: A little over an hour on the high-speed train. You come home Mondays and leave Tuesdays, out of step with everyone's weekend. Nanjing has more surgeries, and half of the extra pay goes on rent.

options.label: Stay in Xuzhou
options.result: You thank him. He comes back next month, and the tray is still yours.

c_manager.title: Applying for Clinic Nursing Supervisor
c_manager.situation: The manager takes you aside: the Clinic Nursing Supervisor is leaving. The job is scheduling, inventory, inspections, standing between dentists and consultants, and no more chairside work. Your commissions go, replaced by a flat allowance.

options.label: Take it
options.result: Your hands move from the instrument tray to the rota. In the first month two dentists come to you separately over the Saturday chairs, each to tell you what's wrong with the other.

options.label: Stay at the chair
options.result: You say your hands want a few more years. The new supervisor is six years younger than you, and comes by every Friday to ask how to file the supply order so it doesn't bounce.

c_rep.title: The instrument salesman
c_rep.situation: The salesman who delivers your burs says his company wants a clinical trainer for northern Jiangsu, someone who knows the chairside. Better base salary, lots of travel, and no more smell of clove oil and sodium hypochlorite.

options.label: Change jobs
options.end: You hang up your scrubs and put on a jacket with a company logo. You start driving the expressways of northern Jiangsu from clinic to clinic, teaching other people's assistants to use the things you've been using for over a decade.

options.label: Stay an assistant
options.result: You say you'll think about it. Next time he delivers burs, he brings you an extra box of hand cream.

c_close.title: The branch is being merged
c_close.situation: A notice from the group: two branches within three kilometers will be merged, and yours will close. You can transfer to the one in the development zone, fifty minutes further each way, or take the statutory severance and go. The new branch wants someone who can bring people up.

options.label: Take the severance
options.end: On the day the branch closes, the six dental chairs are hauled away, leaving six squares of floor tile a little newer than the rest. You take the payout, and the next year you are at the registration window of a community health center.
options.result: You sign and fold up more than ten years of scrubs.

options.label: Go to the new branch
options.result: Fifty more minutes on the bus. You set up the new sterilization room from scratch, using your own way of keeping the log.

endings.retire: Your retirement paperwork goes through on a Monday, the clinic's day off, and your account in the system becomes “departed.” Sterilization is scanned now; the kind of log you kept for over thirty years sits in a filing cabinet in order of year, to be destroyed when the required retention period is up. Chair 3 is empty that day, and happens to be set at exactly the height you like.
endings.burnout: After your neck starts numbing your fingers, you try two more months at the chair. Your hand begins to shake when you pass instruments, and an unsteady hand can't be near someone else's mouth. You talk to the manager and sign out. For the first time, Monday and Sunday are the same.

stages: Mornings in the sterilization room, afternoons at the chair. You scrub instruments, pouch them and log them, and each week your trainer spot-checks your seals and indicators. At the chair you stand on the left with the suction tube and watch the dentist's hands. When a patient asks if it will hurt, all you can say is, let me ask for you.

You run your own chair now: laying out trays against the day's appointments, one set for root canals, one for fillings, one for extractions; mixing, taking impressions, pouring models, sending lab slips, making follow-up calls. Your relationship with the dentist is that he doesn't need to speak. Your relationship with the consultant is that when she speaks, you don't chime in.

You've moved up to implants. Sterile drapes, the implant's batch sticker on the surgical record, forty-odd instruments on the tray, none of them to be wrong. The clinic's infection-control log is yours. A new assistant stands behind you learning to pouch, and you've learned not to take the work out of her hands, only to unseal and redo the pack when she turns away.

You seldom wear gloves anymore. Each week you assign chairs, count supplies and reconcile accounts with the lab. Dentists want Saturdays, consultants want the prime slots, the manager wants revenue per square meter. You accompany the health inspectors and take the complaints. In your hands are a rota, the inventory ERP and a sheaf of inspection checklists. People used to chase you; now you chase them.

You visit four or five clinics a week, going first to the sterilization room and then to the chairside trays. You carry the group's quality form, score every item, then sit down with the manager to discuss the score. You write training slides, set procedures for new equipment, and decide whether a clinic's infection-control lead should be replaced.
work: Your trainer dumps out half of the twenty packs you sealed: there's a crease in the seam. She holds a ruler to it and says steam can't get through there. By the time you've resealed them all it's eight-thirty.
You run a rinse cup for a patient for the first time and the water is too cold; the old lady's teeth jump. The assistant at the next chair tells you the switch has to go all the way to the left.
Monday delivery: you check the packing slip item by item. Burs, root canal files, cotton rolls, sodium hypochlorite. A box of size 15 files is two short, and you chase the courier down the stairs.

A patient with a strong gag reflex needs a lower impression. You have him lift his feet off the chair and count aloud. The tray is in for forty seconds, the margins come out whole, and the dentist nods.

The day after a wisdom tooth comes out, you make the follow-up call, and a college student says it's still oozing. You find out how long and how much gauze, you tell the dentist, and half an hour later he's back in the chair.
The lab returns a model, saying the bite record is off. You compare the wax with that day's notes: you had left and right reversed. You call the technician to apologize, and book the patient again.

Before an implant surgery you read the checklist aloud with the dentist: name, tooth position, implant diameter and length, batch. The box is off from the record by one digit, and you have the circulating nurse swap it.

A new assistant asks in the sterilization room whether this indicator card counts as turned. You tape last week's failed one to the wall and have her compare. It works better than saying it a hundred times.

A patient in his seventies has high blood pressure before surgery, and the family is pressing for today. You bring the monitor readings to the dentist and the surgery is rescheduled. In the corridor the family say some hard things to you.

The ERP shows one impression material being used thirty percent faster than last quarter. You watch at each chair for two days; one dentist squeezes out an extra length every time. You switch to a smaller nozzle and never raise the subject.

Two dentists both want Saturday morning. You pull the structure of the appointments, put implants in the morning and orthodontics in the afternoon, and show each of them a chart. Neither is pleased; both accept it.

The sterilization records at the Xinyi branch are too clean, three months without a single correction. You look at the printouts and the times don't match. You sit down with the manager and start by asking whether the autoclave has been repaired in those three months.

You teach four-handed technique to the region's assistants and play an old video of yourself with the wrong stance. The room dissolves in laughter, and nobody's attention wanders for the rest of the class.
past: After the high school entrance exam, at home in Suining County, your mother says nursing will always put food on the table. You apply to the nursing school in Xuzhou. You pick dental because the other tracks work nights.
Your first practical class is suction on a phantom head. The silicone skull has a fake tongue in its mouth, and you keep sucking it up. Real people move, the teacher says. They're harder.
You intern in the dental department of a public hospital, and the head nurse has you wash instruments for four months. You have to know what dirty looks like first, she says.

You miss the registration deadline for the nursing exam before graduation. Classmates head for Nanjing and Suzhou. You want to stay close to home, and send applications to a few private dental clinics in Xuzhou.
The chain's interview is in a clinic break room. The manager has you hold out your hands to check your nails, and asks if you can work weekends. You say yes. Mondays off, she says.

late.pension_note: Estimate: years of contributions at the low end of Xuzhou's social insurance base leave the pension well below your final monthly income; commissions don't count.
scenes: For the first time you find out what Xuzhou looks like on a Saturday morning. The market is packed with people on their day off. You walk slowly with a bunch of chives, still not quite used to it.

The community health station wants someone to help old people clean their dentures, two mornings a week for thirty yuan in travel money. You can hear from the whistle in an old man's speech that his set needs adjusting.
The wire in your ear is still there, a little under the pitch of the old handpiece. At night you treat it as the sound of a refrigerator, one with no electric bill.

Dental clinics now advertise implant robots, and the thirty-nine-yuan cleaning has gone up to fifty-nine. Walking by, you see the sterilization room has been turned into a glass box for patients to tour. There's a crease in one of the pouches, visible even through the glass.

On the wall at the rehab clinic is a neck exercise chart, the same picture you once taped up in the sterilization room. You do the moves better than anyone. The therapist asks if you've practiced. In a way, you say.

You work behind a pharmacy counter, eyes level, no need to bend your head, and your neck improves a little. People buying toothpaste ask which is best. Any of them, you say. Just don't brush too hard.

The numbness in your fingers comes and goes. You can't handle fine things; threading a needle takes glasses and luck. You've learned to open jars left-handed. The right hand counts only in good weather.

For six months you can't smell clove oil, and your nose feels the lack. Your new coworkers don't know what you used to do. When someone is about to hand you something, your hand is out and waiting well before it gets there.

At the window, in the training room, at the service area, mouths everywhere are talking. You hear the words and look at the teeth: crowded lower front, overdue for a cleaning, and that veneer isn't right.

There are more dental clinics in Xuzhou now than breakfast stalls. When your tooth aches you pick a cheap one, lie back and take in the lamp, the placement of the suction tube, the assistant's hands. She's good. You don't tell her.
Watching TV, you spend half the time on the lead actor's front teeth. That one's shape isn't natural, it's bonded on, and by the second episode you've lost the plot.
The chopsticks in your holder all point the same way, and the bowls are stacked by size on the side that's handy. Your family tells you to leave it. All right, you say. Your hand is already there.

closing.retire: Monday morning, not many people by Yunlong Lake. You are in no hurry. The whine of the handpiece is in your ears, mixed up with the wind off the water.
closing.burnout: The pharmacy's glass doors open and close. You look out at the street with your eyes level. This angle used to be the patients'.
closing.end: Down to the last of the toothpaste, you roll the tube up from the bottom, flat and even, without a single crease in the seal.
